{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{redirect|Bicomplex|the type of number|Bicomplex number}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[Homological algebra]], a '''double complex''' is a generalization of a [[chain complex]] where instead of having a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-grading, the objects in the bicomplex have a <math>\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}</math>-grading. The most general definition of a double complex, or a bicomplex, is given with objects in an [[additive category]] <math>\mathcal{A}</math>. A bicomplex<ref>{{Cite web|title=Section 12.18 (0FNB): Double complexes and associated total complexes—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FNB|access-date=2021-07-08|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref> is a sequence of objects <math>C_{p,q} \in \text{Ob}(\mathcal{A})</math> with two differentials, the '''horizontal differential'''<blockquote><math>d^h: C_{p,q} \to C_{p+1,q}</math></blockquote>and the '''vertical differential'''<blockquote><math>d^v:C_{p,q} \to C_{p,q+1}</math></blockquote>which have the compatibility relation<blockquote><math>d_h\circ d_v = d_v\circ d_h</math></blockquote>Hence a double complex is a [[commutative diagram]] of the form<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
 & & \vdots & & \vdots & &  \\
 & & \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \\
\cdots & \to & C_{p,q+1} & \to & C_{p+1,q+1} & \to & \cdots \\
& & \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \\
\cdots & \to & C_{p,q} & \to & C_{p+1,q} & \to & \cdots \\
& & \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \\
 & & \vdots & & \vdots & &  \\

\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where the rows and columns form chain complexes.

Some authors<ref>{{Cite book|last=Weibel|first=Charles A.|author-link=Charles Weibel|title=An introduction to homological algebra|date=1994|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-64863-9|location=Cambridge [England]|oclc=847527211}}</ref> instead require that the squares anticommute. That is

<blockquote><math>d_h\circ d_v + d_v\circ d_h = 0.</math></blockquote>

This eases the definition of [[Total Complexes]]. By setting <math>f_{p,q} = (-1)^p d^v_{p,q} \colon C_{p,q} \to C_{p,q-1}</math>, we can switch between having commutativity and anticommutativity. If the commutative definition is used, this alternating sign will have to show up in the definition of Total Complexes.

== Examples ==
There are many natural examples of bicomplexes that come up in nature. In particular, for a [[Lie groupoid]], there is a bicomplex associated to it<ref name=":0">{{cite arXiv|eprint=0803.1529|class=math.QA|first1=Jonathan|last1=Block|first2=Calder|last2=Daenzer|title=Mukai duality for gerbes with connection|date=2009-01-09}}</ref><sup>pg 7-8</sup> which can be used to construct its [[De Rham cohomology|de-Rham complex]].

Another common example of bicomplexes are in [[Hodge theory]], where on an [[almost complex manifold]] <math>X</math> there's a bicomplex of differential forms <math>\Omega^{p,q}(X)</math> whose components are linear or anti-linear. For example, if <math>z_1,z_2</math> are the complex coordinates of <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> and <math>\overline{z}_1,\overline{z}_2</math> are the complex conjugate of these coordinates, a <math>(1,1)</math>-form is of the form<blockquote><math>f_{a,b}dz_a\wedge d\overline{z}_b</math></blockquote>
